questions.question: What privacy problem are mix networks primarily designed to mitigate?
options: Metadata correlation (linking senders to recipients via timing/volume/size)
Recovering plaintext from ciphertext without the key
Detecting message tampering on an authenticated channel
Reducing network latency by choosing the shortest path
questions.explanation: Mixnets target traffic analysis: even with strong encryption, an observer can often link who talks to whom using metadata. Mixnets try to break those links with batching, shuffling, and delay.

questions.question: If a mix takes a batch of size B and outputs a uniformly random permutation, how many input↔output matchings are possible (ignoring side channels)?
options: B
B!
questions.explanation: A shuffle chooses one of B! permutations. Real systems still leak via timing and size, but B! captures the combinatorics of the mapping alone.

questions.question: Why do mixnets push hard for fixed-size packets (cells)?
options: To make encryption faster by using shorter keys
To prevent trivial linking by message length/shape
To guarantee HMAC verification succeeds
To ensure packets always take the same route
questions.explanation: If packet sizes differ, an observer can often match inputs and outputs by length even after shuffling. Fixed-size cells remove an easy side-channel.

questions.question: In this lesson’s toy onion packet, why does each layer include an HMAC over (nonce || ciphertext)?
options: To compress ciphertext so batches are smaller
To detect tampering and reject modified packets
To allow the receiver to recover the nonce from ciphertext
To make decryption constant-time automatically
questions.explanation: Without an integrity check, an attacker can flip bits or inject crafted packets that may leak information or break processing. HMAC lets the hop reject invalid packets early.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes onion routing (Tor-like) from mixnets?
options: Onion routing encrypts content; mixnets do not encrypt content
Onion routing aims for low latency; mixnets trade latency for stronger metadata mixing
Onion routing uses public keys; mixnets use only symmetric keys
Onion routing prevents global observers; mixnets only work against local observers
questions.explanation: Both can use layered encryption, but onion routing is typically low-latency and forwards immediately. Mixnets batch and often delay to disrupt timing correlation.

questions.question: What is the most direct consequence of using very small or irregular batches in a mix network?
options: The anonymity set shrinks, making correlation attacks easier
Ciphertexts stop decrypting because the HMAC key changes
Packets become larger because padding becomes impossible
Key derivation stops working because SHA-256 requires batches
questions.explanation: Shuffling only helps when multiple plausible mappings exist. Small batches give attackers far fewer possibilities and make timing analysis much more effective.

questions.question: A classic active attack on naive mix systems is to replay or duplicate messages and watch which outputs repeat. What missing defense does this exploit?
options: Lack of replay/duplicate detection at mixes
Use of fixed-size cells instead of variable-size packets
Use of batching instead of single-message forwarding
Use of multiple hops instead of a single hop
questions.explanation: If mixes accept duplicates, an attacker can tag traffic by repetition and shrink the anonymity set. Production mixnets include replay protection and other tagging defenses.

questions.question: Why do multiple mix hops (multiple independent shuffles) generally increase unlinkability compared to a single hop?
options: Because the attacker must account for a composition of unknown permutations (and often delays), not just one
Because HMAC becomes stronger when applied three times
Because SHA-256 outputs become uniformly random only after three rounds
Because packet padding is unnecessary when you have multiple hops
questions.explanation: With multiple hops, the observed mapping is the composition of several hidden shuffles (and any timing noise). This makes correlation harder unless the attacker can observe and model everything perfectly.
